topic: Agent Skills Supply Chain Security: Protecting Modular AI Workflows in 2026

competitors.title: Skill Issues: How We Discovered Supply Chain Attack Vectors in an AI Agent Skills Marketplace
key_points: Orca researched a major AI agent skills marketplace and found four exploitable primitives: install count inflation, non-deterministic scanning, silent skill override, and blind bulk updates.
Attack flows include bait-and-switch, nested skill injection, and delayed weaponization through a later update.
The research frames skills as first-class supply chain dependencies comparable to package managers, container registries, and CI/CD pipelines.
Recommended marketplace controls: authenticated install telemetry, continuous scanning, warnings for name collisions, and per-skill auditable updates with diffs or changelogs.

competitors.title: Securing AI agents: When AI tools move from reading to acting
key_points: Microsoft maps MCP tool poisoning to OWASP Agentic AI risks ASI02 Tool Misuse and ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities.
The article shows how a changed MCP tool description can silently redirect an enterprise agent to gather and exfiltrate financial records while every individual action appears authorized.
Tool descriptions should be treated like system prompts because agents read them as instructions during planning and tool selection.

Recommended controls include approved MCP publisher/server allowlists, metadata review, DLP on tool call parameters, human approval for high-impact actions, non-human agent identities, Conditional Access, and Sentinel correlation.

competitors.title: OpenClaw's Skill Marketplace and the Emerging AI Supply Chain Threat
key_points: Unit 42 describes OpenClaw as an AI agent that executes third-party skills from ClawHub, making the marketplace a critical agentic software supply chain link.
February-May 2026 analysis found five unblocked malicious or evasive skills despite ClawHub adding VirusTotal and ClawScan screening after earlier campaigns.
Threat categories included macOS infostealers, scanner-threshold evasion, runtime affiliate injection, and agentic front-running.
The finding is useful for showing that skill scanning reduces but does not eliminate marketplace risk, especially for evasive and runtime behaviors.

competitors.title: Socket Brings Supply Chain Security to skills.sh
key_points: Socket says skills.sh had indexed 60,000+ unique skills across Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, and other agent tools as of February 2026.
Skills are decentralized Git-hosted packages that may include natural language instructions plus scripts in Python, JavaScript, shell, or other ecosystems.
Socket highlights why skill scanning is harder than normal dependency scanning: malicious behavior may be several layers deep in referenced scripts rather than in the Markdown description.
Their benchmark reports 94.5% precision, 98.7% recall, and 96.7% F1 against 382 known malicious skills and 355 benign popular skills.

competitors.title: Agent Skills: Explore security threats and controls
key_points: Red Hat explains the Agent Skills structure: a folder with a required SKILL.md file, YAML frontmatter, Markdown instructions, and optional files.
The article identifies filesystem modification, malicious or vulnerable scripts, prompt injection, and credential exposure as core skill risks.
Controls combine traditional secure development practices such as strict permissions, code review, and scanning with AI-specific guardrails, sandboxing, and controlled permissions.
Red Hat notes allowed-tools and signed skill registries as early-stage mechanisms for safer deployment.

competitors.title: Formal Analysis and Supply Chain Security for Agentic AI Skills
key_points: The SkillFortify paper formalizes a five-phase skill lifecycle threat model and argues that heuristic scanners cannot prove absence of malicious behavior.
It cites a January 2026 scan of 42,447 agent skills where 26.1% had at least one vulnerability across 14 vulnerability patterns.
It cites a February 2026 scan of 98,380 skills across multiple agent platforms with 157 confirmed malicious entries.

SkillFortifyBench includes 540 labeled skills across Claude, MCP, and OpenClaw formats, with malicious cases covering data exfiltration, credential theft, arbitrary code execution, prompt injection, reverse shells, typosquatting, dependency confusion, and obfuscated payloads.

competitors.title: The Agent Skills Ecosystem in 2026: Who's Building, What's Working, and What's Next
key_points: Reports that Anthropic launched Agent Skills in October 2025 and published the spec as an open standard at agentskills.io on December 18, 2025.
As of June 2026, roughly 40 skills-compatible products appear in the Agent Skills showcase, including OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI, VS Code, and Claude Code.
Community directories are scaling quickly; SkillsMP reportedly indexed about 1.9 million public skills scraped from GitHub.
This supports the article's scale argument: skills are moving from vendor feature to shared infrastructure, which turns skill provenance into a cross-platform security problem.

competitors.title: Agent Skills Specification
key_points: Official specification defines a skill as a directory with required SKILL.md and optional scripts, references, assets, and other files.
SKILL.md frontmatter requires name and description; optional fields include license, compatibility, metadata, and experimental allowed-tools.
Skills use progressive disclosure: agents load name and description at startup, then full instructions and referenced resources only when a task calls for them.
Security implication: the discovery metadata, full Markdown instructions, optional scripts, and referenced files are all potential control points for validation and policy enforcement.

competitors.title: AI Agent Skills: The New Standard for Modular AI Workflows
key_points: Backslash positions skills as lightweight, external files that can be updated, swapped, or deleted without retraining a model.
The article notes that skills can be stored at project, personal, or system level, creating multiple governance scopes for enterprise teams.
Static skills are pure text instructions, while dynamic skills can reference scripts that the agent may execute depending on task context.
Cross-platform interoperability across Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, and other clients is a productivity benefit and a supply chain propagation risk.

angles: Agent Skills are not just prompts: they are portable, updateable, executable supply chain dependencies that can change agent behavior across tools.
The risk model changes at activation time: discovery metadata looks harmless, but full SKILL.md content, referenced files, and scripts load only when the agent decides they are relevant.
Skill marketplaces are repeating early package registry mistakes: vanity metrics, weak provenance, name collisions, coarse update flows, and scan-once assumptions.
MCP and skills share the same governance problem: natural-language metadata is executable influence because agents treat descriptions and instructions as planning context.
Cross-platform compatibility is a double-edged sword: a useful skill can travel across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and VS Code, but so can a malicious pattern.
Security teams should treat skills like code dependencies, not like documentation: pin versions, review diffs, scan referenced files, restrict execution, and monitor runtime behavior.

Static skills and dynamic skills need different controls: text-only instructions need prompt-injection and policy review, while script-backed skills need malware, secrets, egress, and sandbox controls.

Signed registries and allowed-tools are necessary but immature; enterprises still need local policy enforcement, runtime approvals, and inventory across personal, project, and system skill directories.
A practical enterprise framework is inventory, provenance, permissioning, scanning, update review, runtime monitoring, and incident response for every installed skill.
The highest-risk scenario is delayed weaponization: a trusted skill becomes malicious after reputation, adoption, or marketplace approval is already established.
